title: "बसाइ“ उपन्यासमा नीतिपरक वक्रता "Basai" Upanyasma Neetiparak Bakrata
nepali: पौरस्त्य काव्यचिन्तक कुन्तकद्वारा प्रवर्तित नीतिपरक वस्तुवक्रताको उपयोग गरीलीलबहादुर क्षेत्रीद्वारा रचित बसाइँ उपन्यासको प्रायोगिक अध्ययनमा केन्द्रित यस आलेखमासर्वप्रथम नीतिपरक वस्तुवक्रताको सैद्धान्तिक पर्याधार निर्माण गरी तदनुकूल ईश्वर, धनसम्पति,पश्चात्ताप, मानवता, पुनर्जन्म र परलोक, धर्मसंस्कृतिका उपकरणअनुसार शोध्य कृतिबाटसङ्कलित सामग्रीको विश्लेषण गरिएको छ । यसमा ईश्वर वा विधाता जे भए पनि मानिसउसकै संयोगवियोग वा खटनपटनको चर्चामा ईश्वरप्रतिको आस्था, सोझा गरिब किसानलाईफसाई सम्पत्ति हडप्न खोज्ने नन्दे ढकाल र बैदार बुढाका कार्यमा सम्पत्तिप्रतिको मोह,जानेर वा नजानेर विगतमा गरिएका कार्य र त्यसका परिणामबाट झुमा, मैना, धने आदिकाकथनमा पश्चात्ताप, मोटेकार्कीले धनेप्रति देखाएको उदारता र गाउँघरमा गरेको सहयोग तथातेर्से लामिछानेले धनेप्रति देखाएको सहानुभूतिमा मानवता, पूर्वजन्मका कारण यस जन्ममागरिबहरूको अवस्था पशुतुल्य रहेको तथा सामन्तहरू आनन्ददायी भवनमा रहेको अभिव्यक्तिमा पूर्वजन्म तथा बैदार बुढाको धार्मिक आस्था तथा धामीझाँक्रीको झारफुकजस्ता धर्मसंस्कृतिको चित्रणमा नीतिपरक वस्तुवक्रताको प्रयोग पाइन्छ । तसर्थ विवेच्य कृति नीतिपरक वस्तुसौन्दर्यकादृष्टिले उत्कृष्ट रहेको पुष्टि हुन्छ ।
american_english: This article, focused on a practical study of the novel Basai written by Leelabahadur Kshetri through the use of the ethical vastuvakratā (object-obliquity) propounded by the Eastern poetics thinker Kuntaka, first constructs a theoretical groundwork of ethical vastuvakratā and then, in keeping with it, analyzes the material collected from the work under study according to the devices of God, wealth and property, repentance, humanity, rebirth and the next world, and religion and culture. In it, the use of ethical vastuvakratā is found in the faith in God expressed in the discussion of God or the creator—whatever he may be—and of people's chance unions and separations or their appointments and disposals; in the attachment to property shown in the deeds of Nande Dhakal and Baidar Budha, who try to trap simple poor farmers and seize their property; in the repentance in the words of Jhumā, Mainā, Dhane and others at the deeds done knowingly or unknowingly in the past and their consequences; in the humanity shown in Motekārki's generosity toward Dhane and the help he gave in the village and in Terse Lāmichāne's sympathy toward Dhane; in the previous birth expressed in the statement that because of a previous birth the poor are in an animal-like condition in this birth while the feudal lords are in pleasant buildings; and in the depiction of religious culture such as Baidar Budha's religious faith and the shaman's jhāraphuk. Therefore, it is confirmed that the work under discussion is excellent from the standpoint of ethical vastu-saundarya (object beauty).
british_english: This article, centred on a practical study of the novel Basai written by Leelabahadur Kshetri through the use of the ethical vastuvakratā (object-obliquity) initiated by the Eastern poetics thinker Kuntaka, first builds up the theoretical groundwork of ethical vastuvakratā and, in accordance with that, examines the material gathered from the work under study under the headings of the devices of God, wealth and property, repentance, humanity, rebirth and the world hereafter, and religion and culture. Here the employment of ethical vastuvakratā is to be seen in the faith in God voiced in the discussion of God or the creator, be he what he may, and of people's chance unions and separations or their ordering and disposing; in the attachment to property manifested in the deeds of Nande Dhakal and Baidar Budha, who seek to trap simple poor peasants and lay hold of their property; in the repentance expressed in the words of Jhumā, Mainā, Dhane and others concerning deeds done knowingly or unknowingly in the past and their consequences; in the humanity displayed in Motekārki's generosity towards Dhane and the assistance he rendered about the village, and in the sympathy Terse Lāmichāne showed towards Dhane; in the previous birth set out in the statement that by reason of a former birth the poor are reduced to a beast-like condition in this birth while the feudal lords abide in pleasurable mansions; and in the portrayal of religious culture such as Baidar Budha's religious faith and the jhāraphuk of the dhāmi-jhākri. Consequently, it stands confirmed that the work under discussion is excellent from the point of view of ethical vastu-saundarya (object beauty).
australian_english: This article centres on a practical study of the novel Basai by Leelabahadur Kshetri using the ethical vastuvakratā (object-obliquity) put forward by the Eastern poetics thinker Kuntaka; it first sets up the theoretical groundwork for ethical vastuvakratā and then, in line with that, works through the material gathered from the work under study under the devices of God, wealth and property, repentance, humanity, rebirth and the next world, and religion and culture. In it, ethical vastuvakratā comes through in the faith in God talked about whenever the discussion turns to God or the creator, whoever he may be, and to people's chance unions and separations or their comings and goings; in the fondness for property in the doings of Nande Dhakal and Baidar Budha, who try to rope in simple poor farmers and seize what they own; in the repentance in what Jhumā, Mainā, Dhane and the others say about deeds done knowingly or not in the past and what came of them; in the humanity in Motekārki's generosity towards Dhane and the hand he lent about the village, and in the sympathy Terse Lāmichāne showed towards Dhane; in the former birth put forward in the line that the poor are in a beast-like state in this birth because of a past one while the big landowners are in comfortable houses; and in the picture of religious culture such as Baidar Budha's religious faith and the shaman's jhāraphuk. So it's confirmed that the work under discussion is a cut above the rest from the standpoint of ethical vastu-saundarya (object beauty).
informal_english: This piece takes a practical look at Leelabahadur Kshetri's novel Basai through the ethical vastuvakratā (object-obliquity) thought up by the Eastern poetics man Kuntaka. First it lays out the theory behind ethical vastuvakratā, then works through the material pulled from the novel under the headings God, wealth and property, repentance, humanity, rebirth and the next world, and religion and culture. You can see ethical vastuvakratā at work in all sorts of places: the faith in God that comes up whenever people talk about God or the creator, whatever he is, and about folk's lucky meetings and partings or their comings and goings; in the pull of property in what Nande Dhakal and Baidar Budha get up to, trying to trap simple poor farmers and grab their land; in the repentance in what Jhumā, Mainā, Dhane and the rest say about deeds done knowingly or not in the past and the results of them; in the humanity in Motekārki's generosity towards Dhane and the help he gave round the village, and in the sympathy Terse Lāmichāne showed Dhane; the previous birth in the line about how the poor end up like animals this time round because of a past life while the big landowners sit in comfortable houses; and the religious culture in things like Baidar Budha's faith and the shaman's jhāraphuk. That confirms it: the work under discussion is excellent from the standpoint of ethical vastu-saundarya (object beauty).
translator_notes: Source is a literary analysis of the novel Basai by Leelabahadur Kshetri; technical term nītiparaka vastuvakratā (ethical object-obliquity) from Kuntaka's poetics preserved; clause and sentence order kept as in source.
